findings.title: Write lock acquired without re-checking the cache, so concurrent cold-start requests each re-read the manifest
findings.body: GetWebAssets checks `ret != nil` under the read lock (lines 41-47) and, if empty, unconditionally takes the write lock at line 48 and recomputes the assets without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache` after acquiring the lock. Two (or N) concurrent requests arriving while the cache is empty all observe `ret == nil`, then serialize on the write mutex, and each in turn performs a full `readWebAssetsFromFile` (or CDN fetch) and overwrites the cache. On a cold cache under load this means N sequential disk reads/JSON decodes instead of one, and each request's latency is multiplied by the number of queued callers because the lock is held for the entire IO. The standard fix is to re-check the shared state under the write lock (and return it if already populated) before doing the work, or to only compute outside the lock and swap under it, so exactly one goroutine populates the cache.

findings.title: In Dev mode every request holds the exclusive write lock during file IO, serializing all callers
findings.body: When `cfg.Env == setting.Dev` the early return at line 45 is skipped, so every call now takes the exclusive `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` and holds it for the whole `os.Open` + JSON decode (and potentially the HTTP round-trip to the CDN if the `cdn` branch is ever enabled). Previously concurrent dev requests read the manifest in parallel. Since dev mode intentionally re-reads on every request, a page load issuing several asset requests will now serialize them on this mutex, and a slow/failed read stalls all other callers. If the intent is to always refresh in dev, read/build the result before taking the lock and only swap the pointer (and/or use singleflight to collapse concurrent refresh work) so the critical section contains only the assignment rather than blocking IO.
